title: Provide first aid as an advanced first responder

lessons.title: Principles, preparedness and the body
lessons.html:
Important

This material supports a formal course. Advanced first aid skills must be learnt and assessed hands-on with an accredited first aid training provider, and kept current through refresher training.

Principles of advanced first aid

  • Preserve life, prevent deterioration, promote recovery.
  • Work within your scope of training. You are a first responder, not a paramedic or doctor.
  • Obtain consent from conscious casualties; for children, from a parent or guardian where possible. In a life-threatening emergency where consent cannot be given, act in the casualty's best interest.
  • Respect confidentiality and dignity; document everything.
  • Protect yourself with gloves, eye protection and a CPR barrier.

Advanced preparedness

On a large farm, estate or agri-processing plant the advanced first aider often leads the first aid response. Preparedness includes:

  • A workplace first aid risk assessment: what injuries and illnesses are likely (machinery trauma, amputations, chemical poisoning, snake bites, heat stroke, drowning, cardiac arrest in older workers).
  • Equipment matched to the risks: stocked first aid kits, trauma dressings, splints, eye-wash, spinal immobilisation aids where trained, an AED, oxygen only if trained and authorised.
  • Emergency plans: who calls, where ambulances meet you on remote roads, GPS points of camps and lands, and transport plans if an ambulance will be delayed.
  • Drills and refresher training for first aiders.
  • Knowledge of workers' relevant medical conditions where shared voluntarily, such as epilepsy, diabetes or allergies.

Body systems and why they matter

SystemFunction and first aid relevance
RespiratoryMoves air in and out; gas exchange in the lungs. Airway obstruction, chest injury or poisoning can stop oxygen supply.
CirculatoryHeart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins. Blood loss and heart failure cause shock.
NervousBrain, spinal cord and nerves control the body. Head and spinal injuries, strokes and seizures affect it. Brain cells begin dying within minutes without oxygen.
MusculoskeletalBones, joints and muscles give support and movement; fractures can damage nearby vessels and nerves.
DigestiveAbdominal injuries can bleed internally with few outward signs.
Skin (integumentary)Barrier and temperature control; burns cause fluid loss and infection.
EndocrineHormones such as insulin; diabetic emergencies cause confusion and collapse.

lessons.title: Managing emergency scenes and disasters
lessons.html:
Scene management

  1. Size up: hazards, number of casualties, mechanism of injury, resources needed.
  2. Safety: isolate machinery (engine off, key out, PTO off), electricity and fuel; control animals and traffic; beware of chemical gases in closed spaces such as silos, slurry pits and grain bins. Never enter a confined space to rescue someone unless trained and equipped; many rescuers die this way.
  3. Call for help early with a clear report: location, incident, number and condition of casualties, hazards.
  4. Take charge: assign tasks to bystanders: phoning, fetching the AED and kit, guiding the ambulance, keeping the crowd back.

Multiple casualties: triage

In a bakkie roll-over carrying workers, a trailer accident or a chemical exposure, there may be more casualties than helpers. Triage means sorting casualties so the most urgent but saveable get help first. A commonly used simple approach:

PriorityDescription
Immediate (red)Life-threatening problems that simple care can address: severe bleeding, breathing difficulty, shock
Urgent (yellow)Serious but stable: fractures, burns without breathing problems
Delayed (green)Walking wounded with minor injuries
Deceased or expectantNo breathing after airway is opened, in a mass-casualty situation
  • Ask everyone who can walk to move to a set point; they become green.
  • Check the rest quickly: breathing, severe bleeding, response. Do only life-saving actions (open airway, control bleeding, recovery position) and move on.
  • Re-check casualties often; priorities change.
  • Hand over a clear count and priority list to arriving emergency services.

Specific farm scenes

  • Entanglement in PTO or augers: stop the machine, isolate it, do not reverse the machine to free the person unless directed by rescuers; control bleeding.
  • Electrical incidents: switch off the supply before touching the casualty; stay well away from fallen power lines and call the electricity supplier.
  • Chemical exposures: protect yourself, move the casualty to fresh air if safe, decontaminate with water, keep the label and safety data sheet for the hospital.
  • Drowning: reach or throw, do not go in unless trained; start CPR with rescue breaths.

lessons.title: Life support for all ages and shock
lessons.html:
Primary life support

Follow current resuscitation protocols as taught by your accredited provider. In summary:

  1. Check danger and response.
  2. Shout for help and send someone for the AED and to phone 10177 or 112.
  3. Open the airway with head tilt and chin lift (jaw thrust if trained and spinal injury suspected).
  4. Check for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
  5. If not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED as soon as available.
AdultChildInfant
Hand positionTwo hands, centre of chestOne or two hands, centre of chestTwo fingers, just below nipple line
Depth5 to 6 cmAbout one third of chest depth (about 5 cm)About one third of chest depth (about 4 cm)
Rate100 to 120 per minute100 to 120 per minute100 to 120 per minute

Allow full chest recoil after each compression and keep interruptions to a minimum. Use the compression-to-breath ratio and initial-breath sequence your course teaches; children and infants usually arrest from breathing problems, so effective rescue breaths are vital. Change compressors about every two minutes to stay effective.

Shock

Causes

  • Hypovolaemic: loss of blood or body fluids: external or internal bleeding, severe burns, severe diarrhoea and vomiting, heat exhaustion.
  • Cardiogenic: the heart cannot pump well, for example a heart attack.
  • Anaphylactic: severe allergic reaction to bee stings, foods or medicines.
  • Septic: overwhelming infection.
  • Neurogenic: spinal cord injury affecting blood vessel control.

Recognition

Rapid weak pulse, rapid shallow breathing, pale cold clammy skin, thirst, restlessness, then confusion and falling level of response. In anaphylaxis also swelling of face and throat, wheeze and hives.

Emergency treatment

  • Call for an ambulance urgently; shock can kill.
  • Treat the cause: control bleeding with direct pressure, haemostatic dressings or a tourniquet if trained and the bleeding is life-threatening from a limb.
  • Lay the casualty flat; raise the legs if there is no leg, pelvis or spinal injury and your protocol allows. For breathing difficulty or cardiogenic shock, a half-sitting position may be more comfortable.
  • For anaphylaxis, help with their adrenaline auto-injector.
  • Keep warm, give nothing by mouth, monitor and record vital signs every few minutes.

Key points

  • Work within your training; consent, confidentiality and self-protection always apply.
  • Plan first aid around real workplace risks, with drills and suitable equipment.
  • Never enter confined spaces or electrical scenes until they are safe.
  • Use triage when casualties outnumber helpers.
  • Know CPR for all ages and the causes and treatment of shock; keep accredited training current.
